torold a linkeket belole: The hard limit is mathematical: 100 MB over 360 seconds permits only 2.222 Mb/s total (decimal MB), or about 2.094 Mb/s for video after retaining 128 kb/s audio. That is an 89.3% reduction from the present 19.5 Mb/s video stream. The calculation follows file size = bitrate × duration ÷ 8.Video Bitrate Calculator — Bitrate & File Size - CalculatorLibVideo Bitrate Calculator | File Size & Duration - CalcBE

The strongest approach—without lowering resolution, bit depth, HDR, or preferably frame rate—is to transcode to H.266/VVC using the slowest/highest-quality software encoder available, preferably Fraunhofer VVenC, with 10-bit 4:2:0 input, perceptual optimization, and a strict average video target around 2,050–2,090 kb/s. VVC is the best compression candidate in the cited high-resolution comparison: it outperformed HEVC and AV1, with approximately 78% average BD-rate savings in that test, versus 63% for AV1 and 53% for HEVC.Performance Comparison of VVC, AV1, HEVC, and AVC for High Resolutions VVenC supports perceptual optimization and two-pass VBR.fraunhoferhhi/vvenc It also accepts 10-bit input, and FFmpeg integration is available through libvvenc.[FFmpeg-devel] [PATCH v4 1/1] avcodec: add external enc libvvenc for H266/VVC[FFmpeg-devel] [PATCH v4 1/1] avcodec: add external enc libvvenc for H266/VVC

A practical workflow is:

1. Inspect the source first:
 ffprobe -v error -show_streams -show_format input.mkv

 Record the exact frame rate, HDR transfer function, BT.2020 primaries/matrix, mastering-display data, MaxCLL/MaxFALL, chroma format, audio channels, and whether there are black bars. Do not scale or convert the pixels.

2. Reserve a safety margin. Target roughly 2,050 kb/s video rather than the theoretical 2,094 kb/s, leaving room for audio, container overhead, subtitles, and metadata. If audio can be re-encoded without compromising the requirement, Opus at 64–96 kb/s saves another 32–64 kb/s; otherwise copy the original audio or use AAC at 128 kb/s.

3. Use VVC 10-bit and two-pass VBR. The exact VVenC option names vary by build, so consult `vvencapp --fullhelp`; its documented feature set includes two-pass rate control.fraunhoferhhi/vvenc Conceptually, configure:
 input: 3840×2160, original FPS, yuv420p10le
 codec: H.266/VVC
 average video bitrate: 2,050–2,090 kb/s
 pass: 1 and 2
 preset: slowest available
 subjective/perceptual optimization: enabled
 GOP: approximately 2–4 seconds, while retaining scene-cut detection
 audio: copy, or separately encode to a small transparent-enough track
 output: an ISO-BMFF/MP4 or Matroska container supported by the intended decoder

 With a current FFmpeg build exposing libvvenc, the final muxing stage is broadly of this form (verify option names with `ffmpeg -h encoder=libvvenc`):
 `ffmpeg -i input.mkv -map 0:v:0 -map 0:a:0 -c:v libvvenc -pix_fmt yuv420p10le -b:v 2050k -c:a copy output.mkv`

 For a two-pass encode, use the VVenC-native two-pass controls or the build’s documented FFmpeg wrapper controls rather than blindly assuming x264/x265 pass syntax.

4. Preserve HDR metadata exactly. Keep BT.2020/PQ (SMPTE ST 2084), 10-bit pixels, mastering-display metadata, and MaxCLL/MaxFALL. FFmpeg explicitly models mastering-display primaries, white point, and minimum/maximum luminance as HDR metadata.libavutil/mastering_display_metadata.hFFmpeg: libavutil/mastering_display_metadata.h Source File Verify the output with `ffprobe`, and compare HDR playback on a real HDR display. Do not use `-pix_fmt yuv420p`, `-color_trc bt709`, or an SDR conversion.

5. If VVC playback is unacceptable, use 10-bit AV1 as the fallback, encoded with SVT-AV1 or a very slow AOM-AV1 build. AV1 has substantially better efficiency than HEVC in comparative testing, but the available high-resolution study still places it behind VVC.Performance Comparison of VVC, AV1 and HEVC on 8-bit and 10-bit contentPerformance Comparison of VVC, AV1, HEVC, and AVC for High Resolutions AV1 HDR metadata support exists, including HDR content-light and mastering-display metadata paths in FFmpeg.[FFmpeg-devel] [PATCH 19/27] cbs_av1: Support manipulating HDR CLL	and MDCV metadata

6. Test several short representative segments—motion, foliage, gradients, dark HDR scenes, highlights, and fine texture—at 1.8, 2.05, and 2.3 Mb/s. Compare at native 4K on the target display, not merely by pausing or pixel-peeping. Select the lowest rate with no objectionable banding, blocking, ringing, detail pumping, or HDR highlight damage, then encode the full file and check that it is below 100 MB.

Important conclusion: no codec can honestly guarantee “near-lossless” or “no noticeable degradation” for every 4K HDR source at this budget. Even the cited VVC result reports an average gain, not a guarantee for an individual clip; VVC’s roughly 40% savings versus HEVC in another high-resolution result would imply that 2.1 Mb/s VVC is only roughly comparable to about 3.5 Mb/s HEVC, far below the source’s 19.5 Mb/s.(PDF) Performance Comparison of VVC, AV1, HEVC, and AVC for High Resolutions If the source is complex 4K60, noisy, grainy, or contains fast motion, the constraints are mutually incompatible. The most powerful valid solution is therefore VVC 10-bit, slow/two-pass perceptual encoding, exact HDR metadata preservation, and rigorous visual validation—not a claim that 100 MB will be visually lossless.

entries.answer:
The hard limit is mathematical: 100 MB over 360 seconds permits only 2.222 Mb/s total (decimal MB), or about 2.094 Mb/s for video after retaining 128 kb/s audio. That is an 89.3% reduction from the present 19.5 Mb/s video stream. The calculation follows file size = bitrate × duration ÷ 8.

The strongest approach—without lowering resolution, bit depth, HDR, or preferably frame rate—is to transcode to H.266/VVC using the slowest/highest-quality software encoder available, preferably Fraunhofer VVenC, with 10-bit 4:2:0 input, perceptual optimization, and a strict average video target around 2,050–2,090 kb/s. VVC is the best compression candidate in the cited high-resolution comparison: it outperformed HEVC and AV1, with approximately 78% average BD-rate savings in that test, versus 63% for AV1 and 53% for HEVC. VVenC supports perceptual optimization and two-pass VBR. It also accepts 10-bit input, and FFmpeg integration is available through libvvenc.

A practical workflow is:

1. Inspect the source first:  
`ffprobe -v error -show_streams -show_format input.mkv`

Record the exact frame rate, HDR transfer function, BT.2020 primaries/matrix, mastering-display data, MaxCLL/MaxFALL, chroma format, audio channels, and whether there are black bars. Do not scale or convert the pixels.

2. Reserve a safety margin. Target roughly 2,050 kb/s video rather than the theoretical 2,094 kb/s, leaving room for audio, container overhead, subtitles, and metadata. If audio can be re-encoded without compromising the requirement, Opus at 64–96 kb/s saves another 32–64 kb/s; otherwise copy the original audio or use AAC at 128 kb/s.

3. Use VVC 10-bit and two-pass VBR. The exact VVenC option names vary by build, so consult `vvencapp --fullhelp`; its documented feature set includes two-pass rate control. Conceptually, configure:

- Input: 3840×2160, original FPS, yuv420p10le
- Codec: H.266/VVC
- Average video bitrate: 2,050–2,090 kb/s
- Pass: 1 and 2
- Preset: slowest available
- Subjective/perceptual optimization: enabled
- GOP: approximately 2–4 seconds, while retaining scene-cut detection
- Audio: copy, or separately encode to a small transparent-enough track
- Output: an ISO-BMFF/MP4 or Matroska container supported by the intended decoder

With a current FFmpeg build exposing libvvenc, the final muxing stage is broadly of this form. Verify option names with `ffmpeg -h encoder=libvvenc`:

`ffmpeg -i input.mkv -map 0:v:0 -map 0:a:0 -c:v libvvenc -pix_fmt yuv420p10le -b:v 2050k -c:a copy output.mkv`

For a two-pass encode, use the VVenC-native two-pass controls or the build’s documented FFmpeg wrapper controls rather than blindly assuming x264/x265 pass syntax.

4. Preserve HDR metadata exactly. Keep BT.2020/PQ (SMPTE ST 2084), 10-bit pixels, mastering-display metadata, and MaxCLL/MaxFALL. Verify the output with `ffprobe`, and compare HDR playback on a real HDR display. Do not use `-pix_fmt yuv420p`, `-color_trc bt709`, or an SDR conversion.

5. If VVC playback is unacceptable, use 10-bit AV1 as the fallback, encoded with SVT-AV1 or a very slow AOM-AV1 build. AV1 has substantially better efficiency than HEVC in comparative testing, but the available high-resolution study still places it behind VVC. AV1 HDR metadata support exists, including HDR content-light and mastering-display metadata paths in FFmpeg.

6. Test several short representative segments—motion, foliage, gradients, dark HDR scenes, highlights, and fine texture—at 1.8, 2.05, and 2.3 Mb/s. Compare at native 4K on the target display, not merely by pausing or pixel-peeping. Select the lowest rate with no objectionable banding, blocking, ringing, detail pumping, or HDR highlight damage, then encode the full file and check that it is below 100 MB.

Important conclusion: no codec can honestly guarantee “near-lossless” or “no noticeable degradation” for every 4K HDR source at this budget. Even the cited VVC result reports an average gain, not a guarantee for an individual clip; VVC’s roughly 40% savings versus HEVC in another high-resolution result would imply that 2.1 Mb/s VVC is only roughly comparable to about 3.5 Mb/s HEVC, far below the source’s 19.5 Mb/s. If the source is complex 4K60, noisy, grainy, or contains fast motion, the constraints are mutually incompatible. The most powerful valid solution is therefore VVC 10-bit, slow/two-pass perceptual encoding, exact HDR metadata preservation, and rigorous visual validation—not a claim that 100 MB will be visually lossless.
